tips.title: Two words means no agreement
tips.body: *Une robe bleue* agrees. *Une robe bleu clair* does not. Adding **clair** or **foncé** takes the agreement away, because a two-word colour is really *d'un bleu clair*, where *bleu* is a **noun**.

tips.title: Marron and orange are things
tips.body: A chestnut and a fruit. Neither ever agrees: *des chaussures marron*, *une robe orange*. But **rose** and **violet** do — they have been colour adjectives for centuries.

tips.title: cet is masculine
tips.body: *Cet* and *cette* are pronounced identically, so in writing choose by the **noun's gender**, never by ear. *Cet imperméable* is masculine; *cette écharpe* is feminine.

tips.title: trop is not très
tips.body: *Trop cher* means you are **not** buying it. *Très cher* means it is expensive and you might. A reading question about whether someone bought something turns on this one word.

tips.title: Sizes use faire
tips.body: **Je fais du 38** — never *je suis 38*. And **la taille** is clothes, **la pointure** is shoes.

steps.title: Dans le magasin
steps.body:
A shop conversation is short and it is nearly always the same. Learn the handful of lines and you can hold the whole exchange.

**The assistant opens:**

- **Je peux vous aider ?** — Can I help you?
- **Vous faites quelle taille ?** — What size are you?

**You reply:**

- **Je cherche un pull.** — I'm looking for a jumper.
- **Je fais du 38.** — I'm a size 38.
- **Je peux l'essayer ?** — Can I try it on?
- **C'est combien ?** — How much is it?
- **Je le prends.** — I'll take it.

**Taille or pointure?** **La taille** is your size in **clothes**. **La pointure** is your size in **shoes**. They are not interchangeable, and an assistant will use whichever one matches what you are holding.

Notice **je fais du 38** — French uses *faire* for sizes, not *être*. *Je suis 38* is not said.

steps.title: Les couleurs s'accordent
steps.body:
A colour is an **adjective**, so it does two things English colours never do: it goes **after** the noun, and it **agrees** with it.

$$\textit{un pull} \; \textbf{vert} \qquad \textit{une robe} \; \textbf{verte} \qquad \textit{des pulls} \; \textbf{verts} \qquad \textit{des robes} \; \textbf{vertes}$$

The pattern is the ordinary one: **+e** for feminine, **+s** for plural, **+es** for both.

**Three things to know beyond that:**

- Colours **already ending in -e** — *rouge, jaune, rose, beige* — do not change in the feminine. They still add **-s** in the plural: *des robes rouges*.
- **gris** already ends in **-s**, so the masculine plural is unchanged: *des pulls gris*. The feminine is **grise**.
- Three are irregular in the feminine: **blanc → blanche**, **violet → violette**, and *gris → grise* as above.

steps.title: Les couleurs qui ne changent jamais
steps.body:
Two groups of colours **never agree at all**. They are worth a step of their own because they look like mistakes when they are right.

**1. Colours that are really nouns.** **Marron** is a chestnut and **orange** is a fruit. A noun borrowed as a colour keeps its own shape:

- *des chaussures* **marron** — brown shoes. Not *marrons*.
- *une robe* **orange** — an orange dress. Not *orangée*.

**2. Colours made of two words.** As soon as a colour is described by a second word, **both parts freeze**:

- *une robe* **bleu clair** — a light blue dress. Not *bleue claire*.
- *des chaussures* **bleu foncé** — dark blue shoes. Not *bleues foncées*.

So *une robe bleue* agrees, and *une robe bleu clair* does not. Adding *clair* takes the agreement away.

**Why it works that way** is worth knowing, because it makes the rule stick: a two-word colour is really a shortening of *d'un bleu clair* — *of a light blue*. Inside that phrase *bleu* is a noun, and the colour of a dress is not itself feminine.

**The exception to remember:** *rose* and *violet* **do** agree, even though roses and violets are also things. They have been colours in French for so long that they behave as ordinary adjectives: *une robe rose*, *une robe violette*.

steps.title: Ce, cet, cette, ces
steps.body:
To point at something in a shop — *this jumper*, *those shoes* — you need the **demonstrative adjective**. There are four forms, and choosing between them is mechanical.

| | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| masculine singular | **ce** | *ce pull* |
| masculine singular before a vowel | **cet** | *cet imperméable* |
| feminine singular | **cette** | *cette robe* |
| any plural | **ces** | *ces chaussures* |

**Cet exists for one reason only:** to stop *ce* running into a vowel. *Ce imperméable* is awkward to say, so French inserts the **t**. It is still masculine — *cet* is not a feminine form, even though it sounds exactly like *cette*.

That last point catches people out in **writing**: *cet* and *cette* are pronounced identically. The way to choose is not by ear but by the noun's gender.

**And ces covers everything plural** — masculine, feminine, both. One form, no thinking required.

steps.title: Trop, assez et le prix
steps.body:
Most of what you say after trying something on is a **judgement**, and judgements need a small set of words.

- **trop** — too. *C'est trop grand.*
- **assez** — quite, or enough. *C'est assez cher.*
- **très** — very. *C'est très joli.*

**Trop is not très.** *C'est trop cher* means it costs more than you will pay; *c'est très cher* means it is expensive and you might still buy it. Examiners use the difference.

**The judgements themselves:**

- *trop grand / trop petit* — too big / too small
- *trop cher* — too expensive
- *trop serré / trop large* — too tight / too loose
- *à la mode* — fashionable
- *démodé* — out of fashion

**Talking about price:**

- **Ça coûte combien ?** or **C'est combien ?** — How much is it?
- **Ça coûte trente euros.** — It costs thirty euros.
- **C'est en solde ?** — Is it reduced?
- **Il y a une réduction de vingt pour cent.** — There's twenty per cent off.
- **Je vais réfléchir.** — I'll think about it. *The polite way to leave without buying.*

And to finish: **Je le prends** (masculine), **Je la prends** (feminine), **Je les prends** (plural). The pronoun matches what you are buying and sits **before** the verb.

steps.title: À toi : au magasin
steps.body:
**Partie A.** Écris la bonne forme de la couleur :

1. une robe (vert)
2. des chaussures (blanc)
3. une chemise (bleu clair)
4. des baskets (marron)

**Partie B.** Écris *ce*, *cet*, *cette* ou *ces* :

5. ___ pull
6. ___ veste
7. ___ imperméable
8. ___ chaussures

**Partie C.**

9. Traduis : *This jacket is too expensive. Do you have it in black?*
10. Écris une conversation de six lignes dans un magasin de vêtements : tu cherches un pull, tu l'essayes, il est trop grand, et tu en demandes un autre.

steps.title: Aller plus loin
steps.body:
**The colour that stops agreeing.** *Une robe bleue* agrees. *Une robe bleu clair* does not. Adding a second word **removes** the agreement, because a two-word colour is a shortening of *d'un bleu clair* — *of a light blue* — and inside that phrase *bleu* is a **noun**. A dress is feminine; the shade of blue is not. Being able to say **why** is what separates a remembered rule from a usable one, and it settles *bleu foncé*, *vert clair* and every other pair without a fresh effort of memory.

**Marron and orange, but not rose and violet.** All four are things as well as colours. The difference is time: *rose* and *violet* have been ordinary colour adjectives in French for centuries and agree normally — *une robe rose*, *une robe violette*. *Marron* and *orange* arrived later and still behave as nouns. There is no rule that predicts this; there are just two words to remember, and remembering **which two** is easier than remembering a list of eight.

**Cet is masculine.** It sounds exactly like *cette*, so in writing it is chosen by gender, never by ear: *cet imperméable* is masculine, *cette écharpe* feminine. If you can hear no difference, ask what the noun's gender is.

**En takes the plain colour.** *Je le voudrais en bleu* — whatever the garment, after *en* the colour does not agree. It is naming the colour, not describing the garment.

**Trop against très.** *Trop cher* rules it out; *très cher* does not. A reading question that asks whether someone bought the item can turn on exactly that word.

**Add a reason, not more adjectives.** In a writing task, *j'ai acheté un pull vert parce qu'il était en solde et que le rouge était trop cher* earns more than three garments with three colours. **One** opinion with a **reason** and a **comparison** does more work than a list, and it lets you bring in a second tense.

**And singular where English is plural.** *Un pantalon*, *un jean*, *un short* are **singular** in French — *mon pantalon est noir*, not *sont*. English treats trousers as two things; French treats them as one.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- **Je cherche…**, **Je peux l'essayer ?**, **C'est combien ?**, **Je le prends.**
- **La taille** is clothes size; **la pointure** is shoe size.
- Sizes use **faire**: *je fais du 38*.
- Colours go **after** the noun and **agree**: *un pull vert*, *une robe verte*, *des robes vertes*.
- Colours already ending in **-e** do not change in the feminine: *une robe rouge*.
- **gris** already ends in **-s**: *des pulls gris*.
- Irregular feminines: **blanche**, **violette**, **grise**.
- **marron** and **orange** never agree — they are nouns.
- A **two-word** colour never agrees: *une robe bleu clair*, *des chaussures bleu foncé*.
- After **en**, the colour stays plain: *en bleu*, *en noir*.
- **ce** / **cet** / **cette** / **ces** — *cet* is masculine, before a vowel only.
- **trop** = too, **très** = very. *Trop cher* means you are not buying it.
- **Je le / la / les prends** — the pronoun matches the item and goes **before** the verb.
- **un pantalon**, **un jean**, **un short** are **singular** in French.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Une conversation complète :**

*— Je cherche une veste, s'il vous plaît.*
*— Vous faites quelle taille ?*
*— **Je fais du 38**. Est-ce que je peux essayer **cette veste verte** ?*
*— Bien sûr.*
*— Ah non, **c'est trop petit**. Est-ce que vous **l'**avez **en noir** ?*
*— Oui, voilà.*
*— C'est combien ? … Parfait, **je la prends**.*

**Ce qui compte ici :**

- **Je fais du 38** — sizes use *faire*, never *être*.
- **Cette veste verte** — *veste* is feminine, so **cette**, and the colour agrees: **verte**.
- **Trop petit** — *trop*, not *très*. *Très petit* would not explain why you are asking for another.
- **En noir** — after *en*, the colour stays plain whatever the garment.
- **L'avez** and **je la prends** — the pronoun goes **before** the verb.

**Pour aller plus loin :** *elle est en solde à trente euros* brings in a price and a reason, and *et en 40 ?* asks for a different size as well as a different colour — two changes in one line, which reads like a real exchange rather than an exercise.

questions.prompt: Explique quand une couleur s'accorde en français et quand elle ne s'accorde pas, et explique pourquoi.
questions.solution: En général, une couleur est un adjectif : elle se place après le nom et elle s'accorde. On écrit donc un pull vert, une robe verte, des pulls verts et des robes vertes. Les couleurs qui se terminent déjà par un e, comme rouge ou jaune, ne changent pas au féminin, mais elles prennent un s au pluriel. Trois couleurs sont irrégulières au féminin : blanc devient blanche, violet devient violette et gris devient grise. Mais il y a deux cas où la couleur ne s'accorde jamais. D'abord, les couleurs qui sont en réalité des noms, comme marron, qui est une châtaigne, et orange, qui est un fruit : on écrit des chaussures marron et une robe orange, sans s. Ensuite, les couleurs composées de deux mots, comme bleu clair ou bleu foncé : on écrit une robe bleu clair, même si robe est féminin. La raison est intéressante : bleu clair est une forme abrégée de d'un bleu clair, et dans cette expression bleu est un nom. C'est la nuance de bleu qui est claire, pas la robe. Enfin, après la préposition en, la couleur reste toujours au masculin singulier, parce qu'on nomme la couleur au lieu de décrire le vêtement : je voudrais cette robe en bleu.

questions.modelAnswer:
**La règle normale.** A colour is an adjective: it goes **after** the noun and **agrees**. *Un pull vert, une robe verte, des pulls verts, des robes vertes.*

**Les cas particuliers.** Colours already ending in **-e** (*rouge, jaune, rose*) do not change in the feminine but still add **-s**. Three are irregular in the feminine: **blanche, violette, grise**.

**Deux cas où la couleur ne s'accorde jamais :**

- **Colours that are really nouns** — *marron* is a chestnut, *orange* a fruit: *des chaussures marron*, *une robe orange*.
- **Two-word colours** — *une robe bleu clair*, *des chaussures bleu foncé*.

**Pourquoi.** *Bleu clair* is short for **d'un bleu clair** — *of a light blue*. Inside that phrase *bleu* is a **noun**, so it is the **shade** that is light, not the dress. That is why adding a word **removes** the agreement, and it settles every pair of this kind at once.

**Et après *en*** the colour is being **named** rather than describing the garment, so it stays plain: *cette robe en bleu*.

examTechnique.body:
Put the colour after the noun and make it agree, unless it is marron, orange, or made of two words.

Check whether the colour has a second word before writing any ending on it.

After en, leave the colour plain: en bleu, en noir.

Choose between cet and cette by the noun's gender, because they sound the same.

Use faire for sizes, and taille for clothes against pointure for shoes.

Decide whether you mean trop or très, since trop rules the purchase out.

In a writing task, give one garment an opinion, a reason and a comparison rather than listing three.
examinerErrors: Writing des chaussures marrons with an s.
Writing une robe bleue claire instead of une robe bleu clair.
Making the colour agree after en, as in en bleue.
Using cette with a masculine noun beginning with a vowel, instead of cet.
Writing je suis 38 instead of je fais du 38.
Using très where trop is meant, which changes whether the item was bought.
Treating un pantalon or un jean as plural.
Putting the colour before the noun, as in une verte robe.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer gets the colour right without hesitating, because it knows the rule has a reason: a two-word colour is a shortened noun phrase, so it cannot agree. It writes *cet* by asking the noun's gender rather than listening. It distinguishes *trop* from *très* and understands that the choice changes the meaning of the sentence, not just its strength. And in a writing task it takes one garment and gives it an opinion, a reason and a comparison across two tenses, rather than listing three garments in three colours.
